_note: R48 families of the realm (moved from marriage.json houses; marriage.json keeps only the marriage rules). Same ids as before, so saves keep their standing. Each house: seat town, major/minor, what it's known for, a goal and a temperament (rules below), a 3-quest thread, perks at Friendly and Allied (minor houses: one perk from Friendly), whether it offers marriage (true, or "allied"), optional `rival` (helping one angers the other). Later rounds add Gilmane (Saltmere, R49), Crane (the usurper, R50) and Clan Brokka (Dwarfhold, R51) the same way.

honest.name: Honest
honest.text: Standing rises steadily from fair deals and requests filled. Breaking a deal (a quest against them) costs a lot.

scheming.text: Offers shady but profitable deals. Standing swings fast, and it may betray you when Cold.

pious.text: Likes Church members and donations, and dislikes Rogues' Guild members.

ruthless.name: Ruthless
ruthless.text: Respects strength (raids won, wars won, bandits cleared). It sneers at gifts (half value).

idealistic.name: Idealistic
idealistic.text: Likes charity and patronage, and hates cruelty (quests against other houses).

proud.name: Proud
proud.text: Slow to warm, quick to take offence, and loyal once Allied.

usurper.name: House Crane
usurper.text: The house that took House Vael's name. Always Rival; no gifts, no marriage, no truce. Chapters 9 and 10 settle it.
usurper._note: R50: House Crane is not in `list` (no drift, troubles, suitors or gifts); it starts Rival and leaves the realm, disgraced, after chapter 10.

dagonLocals._note: R55: Saltmere's locals. One pool per Lodge mood (outsider / tolerated / kin / enemy), 10 lines each.
outsider: A woman gutting fish stops, knife still, and watches you pass without blinking. Her eyes are far too large.
Shutters close one by one as you walk down the street. Somewhere behind them, someone is humming.
‘Market's closed,’ says the stallholder, though the stall is full. ‘For you.’
Two boys on the harbour wall stop talking when you come near, and stay stopped until you are gone.
The innkeeper wipes the same glass for as long as you stand there. He never looks up.
Every door you pass has the same mark scratched over the lintel: a wave, and an eye inside it.
An old man on a bench smells of brine and low tide. His skin is grey and loose at the neck, like wet paper.
You ask the way to the church. Three people answer at once, ‘There is no church,’ and walk off together.
The fog comes in off the sea at noon. Inside it, faces at the windows are just pale circles with dark eyes.
Someone has left a fish on your cart, gutted, its head turned to face the sea.
tolerated: The harbourmaster nods once. It's the first time anyone has.
Nets heavy with silver fish, chests of pearls on the quay. No one here is poor. No one says why.
Above the church door the gold sign of wrong angles catches the light. You look away; your head aches for an hour.
A fishwife sells to you at last, counting the coins twice with long, damp fingers.
The church on the hill is gilded from step to spire. In this fog-grey town it shines like something drowned.
‘Good catch this season,’ a sailor says, without smiling. ‘Always is. We keep our end.’
The carvings on the church door show men kneeling to something in the water. Some of the men have no faces left.
A child offers you a pearl the size of a thumbnail for a copper. Her mother pulls her away, hissing.
At low tide the whole town comes down to the beach and stands still, looking out at the reef.
The bell in the church tower doesn't ring the hours. It rings the tides.
kin: ‘Father provides,’ the fishwife says, pressing a fish into your hand. Her fingers are cold and webbed at the knuckle.
The children sing at the tideline at dusk. You know the words now.
Inside the gilded hall the carvings seem to move when the candles flicker. Tonight it is almost comforting.
Doors open as you pass. ‘Brother,’ someone murmurs, ‘sister,’ and the door closes softly again.
The sign over the altar no longer hurts to look at. That frightens you more than the pain did.
The harbourmaster waves your cart through without a toll. ‘Family,’ he says, and his eyes are very wide.
The old ones on the benches watch the sea with you now, all of you waiting for the same thing.
A gift on your doorstep at dawn: reef-gold worked into a crown no bigger than a ring, still wet.
Someone you don't know calls you by your grandmother's name and asks after Mother.
The water in the harbour is warm tonight, and something under it is singing.
enemy: Someone has painted the wave-and-eye sign on your cart in fish oil.
The whole street turns to watch you, all at once, and says nothing.
A wet handprint on the inn door, too wide, with too many joints.
No one will sell to you. A man spits at your boots, and the spit smells of the sea.
The church doors are open. Every face inside turns to you, and the singing stops.
Your boat's rope has been cut and tied again in a knot no sailor knows.
A child points at you and whispers ‘Father knows’. Her mother doesn't stop her.
At night you hear something wet dragging itself up the road to your door, then back down to the sea.
The fog smells of rot. Shapes stand in it at the end of every street, waiting.
Fish heads on the doorstep, a dozen of them, all looking at the house.
seaKin: “You've the look, you have. Welcome home.”
An old woman touches your cheek. “Father knows you.”
“No charge for you. Not for one of us.”
The fishwives nod as you pass, slow and knowing.
“Your eyes have gone the right colour. Good.”
“When the tide calls, don't be afraid. It's warm down there.”
A child stares, then smiles a too-wide smile.
“The Lodge saved you a seat, near the front.”
“Swim with us at the low tide sometime.”
The barman pours before you ask. “Yours, cousin.”
